卡朗古鼓屬膜鳴樂器，常見於西非格里奧音樂，以夾臂擠壓皮索改變音高，模仿語調與韻律: The kalangu is a membranophone, common in West African griot music, whose pitch is changed by squeezing the leather cords under the arm, imitating speech tones and rhythm. It can play short phrases on its own, and in line-ups with the Yoruba dùndún, the Ashanti atumpan and the fontomfrom it can carry ceremonial messages. Among the Serer the tama drum is used in the wo and xaat traditions, in a drum ensemble with the pengel, lam and cin. After the twentieth century it entered Senegalese mbalax, Nigerian fuji and juju, and appears at weddings, funerals and private ceremonies.
卡朗古鼓採用沙漏形木製共鳴箱，通常由非洲本地硬木雕刻而成。鼓面採用動物皮革（多為: The kalangu has an hourglass-shaped wooden resonator, usually carved from local African hardwood. The heads are of animal hide (mostly cowhide or goatskin), which holds tension well. The two heads are joined by leather tension cords, and the cords can adjust the pitch of the drum. The frame is wood, solid and durable. The leather tension cords are of natural fibre, letting the player control how tight they are with the muscles of the arm and so change the pitch as he plays.
卡朗古鼓為沙漏形膜鳴樂器，演奏時通常夾於腋下，鼓腰置於手臂與肋骨之間。鼓面由張力: The kalangu is an hourglass-shaped membranophone, usually held under the arm when played, with the waist of the drum between the arm and the ribs. The heads are joined by tension cords, and the player squeezes or releases the cords with the arm to change the tension of the heads, giving a higher or a lower pitch; a single stroke can also slide in pitch, producing a vibrato-like effect. A beginner should first steady the hold, then practise controlling the pitch change by how far the arm squeezes, and make the rhythm and the pitch movement follow the tones of the language.
卡朗古鼓為西非沙漏形膜鳴鼓，歷史可追溯至波諾人、約魯巴人、迦納帝國與豪薩人，亦為: The kalangu is a West African hourglass-shaped membranophone drum whose history can be traced to the Bono, the Yoruba, the Ghana Empire and the Hausa, and it is also used by griot musicians. From the eighteenth century drummers sent ceremonial messages and commands by pitch and rhythm over as much as four or five miles; the Yoruba and Ashanti drums could relay them for twenty miles. Among the Serer of Senegal and the Gambia the tama drum is used in the wo and xaat traditions, and griots strike it in war, on royal orders and on special occasions. After the twentieth century it entered West African popular music, such as Senegalese mbalax and Nigerian fuji and juju, and is also found at weddings and funerals and in band line-ups.
卡朗古鼓音色深沉而富有穿透力，具有溫暖的鼓聲特質。其獨特之處在於音高可變性強，通: The kalangu has a deep, carrying timbre, warm in the way of a drum. What is distinctive is how far the pitch can change: by adjusting the tension of the hide it spans a range from low to comparatively sharp, and can imitate the rise and fall of human speech. The double layer of the heads and the way the drum is clamped under the arm produce a rich resonance, so the sound travels well and stays clear. Compared with the heaviness of a Western timpani, the kalangu is more flexible and expressive; compared with other African membranophones its pitch is easier to control and to recognise. Overall it has both the raw texture of drumming and a speech-like expressiveness, which makes it a distinctive talking instrument.
卡朗古鼓（Kalangu）又稱說話鼓，西非膜鳴樂器，H-S 211.242.11: The kalangu (Kalangu), also called the talking drum, is a West African membranophone, H-S 211.242.11. It is hourglass-shaped, with the heads at either end joined by leather tension cords; the player holds it under the arm and squeezes or releases the cords with the arm and body to change the pitch, imitating the tones and rhythm of speech. Traditionally griots and other drummers used it to send messages, for ceremonies and for the king's special occasions; today it also appears in West African popular music, at weddings and funerals and at other events.
